Dear Ms. Barta:

On behalf of Blue Earth County, and as a follow-up to the 401 pre-filing meeting held via Teams with
Ryan Thilges (Blue Earth County) on July 29, 2026, please accept this letter as formal submittal of a
request for a Section 401 Water Quality Certification for the proposed Rapidan Dam Removal Project in
Rapidan Township, Blue Earth County, Minnesota.

This application is being submitted in accordance with Section 401 of the Clean Water Act and Minnesota
Rules Chapter 7050. The proposed project involves the re-establishment of 2,310 linear feet of Blue Earth
River surrounding Rapidan Dam. The proposed stabilization methods will utilize streambank grading,
riprap armoring, riparian vegetation establishment, and native seeding and planting.

Enclosed for your review are the following materials:

    •    Completed Antidegradation Assessment Form

    •    Antidegradation Assessment Form supplemental responses

    •    Required application forms and supporting documentation

    •    Project plans and figures

    •    EAW correspondences

    •    Pre-filing Meeting Confirmation

The project has been designed to avoid and minimize impacts to surface waters to the maximum extent
practicable. Where impacts are unavoidable, appropriate measures are proposed consistent with state
and federal requirements. The applicant believes the project meets applicable water quality standards
and antidegradation requirements.

If additional information or clarification is needed during your review, please contact David Taylor at 720-
464-4985 or dtaylor@barr.com. We appreciate your time and consideration of this request and look
forward to working with MPCA throughout the review process.

Instructions: This form provides general guidance on information that may be necessary for antidegradation review. The Minnesota
Pollution Control Agency (MPCA) reserves the right to request information from the applicant in addition to that provided in this form.
Section 401 of the Clean Water Act requires any applicant for a federal license or permit that authorizes an activity that may result in
a discharge to Waters of the United States to obtain certification from the state or tribe in which the discharge originates to ensure
compliance with applicable water quality standards. In addition to completing the Joint Application Form,
https://bwsr.state.mn.us/joint-application-form, applicants whose proposed projects may require an MPCA Individual 401 Water
Quality Certification for work in aquatic resources must also provide the information necessary to demonstrate compliance with the
Minnesota antidegradation water quality standards (Minn. R. 7050.0265, https://www.revisor.mn.gov/rules/7050.0265/). Applicants
should review the antidegradation requirements in Minn. R. 7050.0285 (https://www.revisor.mn.gov/rules/7050.0285/) prior to
completing this form.
The purpose of the antidegradation requirements is to achieve and maintain the highest possible quality in surface waters of the
state. To accomplish this purpose, antidegradation requires:
         A. The protection of existing uses and the level of water quality necessary to protect existing uses;
         B. The minimization of degradation of high water quality, and only to extent necessary to accommodate important
              economic or social development;
         C. The protection of outstanding resource value waters; and
         D. Consideration of thermal discharges.

Antidegradation Form – Responses
Blue Earth County/Rapidan Dam Removal Project/USACE ID: MVP-2002-03504-DAS

1         Environmental Assessment Worksheet (EAW)/ Environmental Impact
          Statement (EIS)
An Environmental Assessment Worksheet (EAW) was submitted to Minnesota
Environmental Quality Board on September 22, 2026 per 27A, Public waters, public waters
wetlands, and wetlands. The EAW was published on the EQB Monitor on September 29,
2026 and the public comment period ends on October 29, 2026.

2         Analysis of alternatives to project design that avoid or minimize degradation
2.1        Purpose and Need for the Project
The purpose of the Rapidan Dam Removal Project (Project) is to stabilize the banks of the
Blue Earth River after dam removal activities in order to convey normal river ﬂows, re-
establish more natural river functions, and to properly manage future ﬂood events.

The need to re-establish a 2,310-foot section of the Blue Earth River arises from the erosion
of the west embankment and partial failure of the Rapidan Dam following the June 24,
2024, ﬂood event, which compromised and destabilized the dam structure. A feasibility
study for repairing the dam prior to the June 2024 ﬂood event determined that extensive,
costly modiﬁcations would be required to rehabilitate it and restore power production. The
June 2024 ﬂood event caused considerable erosion on the west bank, which ampliﬁes the
need for decommissioning and removing the dam and re-establish a more natural Blue
Earth River ecosystem. The remnants of the dam present multiple concerns:

      •    Public Safety: The remaining structure poses a safety risk to recreational users,
           urban explorers, downstream communities, and infrastructure due to its instability
           and potential for additional failure.

      •    Environmental Degradation: The partially breached dam and resulting river channel
           continue to deflect the river toward the west slope, influencing erosion and
           sediment transport, affecting the ecological function of the river and degrading
           aquatic habitat.

      •    Economic Considerations: Repairing or rehabilitating the dam to its original
           condition would require significant public investment with limited benefit,
           particularly given the outdated purpose and lack of modern utility for the structure.
           Conversely, removal would eliminate ongoing maintenance and liability costs while
           supporting natural resource recovery.



4300 MarketPointe Drive, Suite 200, Minneapolis, MN 55435 | 952.832.2600
 2.2     Project Overview
The Project is located on a combination of privately-owned and publicly-owned properties,
including land owned by Blue Earth County. Blue Earth County has not finalized the west
slope restoration design (Alternative 2) due to delays associated with landowner
coordination. Alternative 2 is the Preferred Alternative and has evolved to a 60% design and
is included in this application package (Attachment 2).

Alternative 2, as described in (Section 3), relies primarily on streambank grading, riprap
armoring, and riparian vegetation establishment, with minimal use of in-stream structures
or in-stream bioengineering methods. Design considerations prioritize immediate bank
stabilization and sediment reduction. Access will be restored to the downstream county
park property along the west side of the river. The channel banks will be reconstructed by
placing suitable fill material in controlled compacted lifts to achieve adequate density and
shear strength for a stable channel bank. This will direct river flow back along its original
alignment and reduce shear stress along the reconstructed west slope. The interface of
embankment and Blue Earth River will be stabilized using riprap armoring, and the
reconstructed embankment will be vegetated to provide resistance to erosion and slope
degradation.

After the Rapidan Dam is completely removed, the east slope will be rebuilt by excavating
flatter slopes and placing adequately sized riprap. The east slope will be graded to
integrate with CSAH 9 bridge replacement project contours. The finished east slope will be
revegetated or otherwise enhanced to provide resistance to erosion and slope
degradation.

2.3     Project Alternatives
Alternatives from the project are discussed in the subsequent sections.
2.3.1    Alternative 1: Dismissed
Description and Design Considerations
Alternative 1 would have restored a long reach of the Blue Earth River by mitigating future
erosion impacts resulting from the removal of Rapidan Dam. This alternative would have
included restoring up to 10,000 feet of the Blue Earth River, requiring extensive grading and
the placement of over 200,000 tons of riprap within the channel.




Expected Performance
 The design proposed grading, contouring, and placement of riprap to reduce ﬂow velocities
and minimize scour, as well as channel widening to improve conveyance of ﬂoodwaters.
However, agencies were concerned that the extensive use of in-channel riprap and
boulders required to achieve these objectives could negatively affect water quality,
particularly pH, and limit the mobility of aquatic organisms. Ongoing maintenance would
also have been a considerable effort with the extensive footprint of the alternative.

Construction, Operation, and Maintenance Costs

The engineer’s opinion of construction cost for this alternative was $89 million. Long-term
maintenance cost were not considered prior to this alternative being rejected.

Reliability

Reliability of this alternative was considered high in terms of bank stabilization and
sediment control. However, this alternative was expected to have greater water quality,
aquatic habitat, and overall total impacts to the Blue Earth River than other alternatives.
2.3.2    Alternative 2 ( Preferred Alternative): Bank Grading with Riprap and Vegetation
         Establishment
See Section 3 for a description of the preferred alternative.
2.3.3    Alternative 4: Bank Grading with Riprap and Vegetation Establishment – Central
         West Bank Parcel Avoidance
Description and Design Considerations
This alternative is a variation of Alternative 2 considered due to landowner constraints
associated with lands in the central portion of the west bank. Alternative 4 was developed
to avoid the private parcel but to allow the project to move forward. Negotiations between
the private landowner and the County have culminated, and access to the central parcel is
available for project development. This alternative utilizes the same channel stabilization
methods (streambank grading, riprap, vegetation establishment) as Alternative 2, but
would have avoided the private parcel on the west bank, leaving an undeveloped void
within the project area.

Expected Performance
Riprap would stabilize eroding banks and substantially reduces sediment inputs to the Blue
Earth River. The proposed grading activities, avoiding the private parcel, would leave a large
void on the landscape and viewshed of the project area. The extensive, unstable slope
would continue to erode over time and provide a public safety hazard.

Construction, Operation, and Maintenance Costs
Initial construction costs would be slightly higher compared to the preferred alternative
due to the difference in amount of grading and material needs. Alternative 4 construction
cost were not fully evaluated but are assumed to similar to Alternative 2, approximately $25
 million, as the designs are similar. Long-term maintenance costs are generally low, as
riprap is durable and resistant to erosive forces once installed.

Reliability
Reliability is high in terms of bank stabilization and sediment control. However, this
alternative leaves a large void on the landscape and viewshed of the area which would be
subject to ongoing erosion. As a result, this alternative is less favorable than Alternative 2.
2.3.4     Alternative 5: Do-Nothing
Description and Design Considerations
Under the no-action alternative, no restoration or stabilization measures would be
implemented. Existing conditions surrounding the damaged Rapidan dam, including
ﬂooding damage and debris, ongoing streambank erosion, and habitat degradation, would
persist. No design considerations or constraints apply.

Expected Performance
This alternative would not reduce sediment loading. The dam would continue to deﬂect
the river toward the west slope, allowing continued degradation of water quality, aquatic
habitat, and channel stability. The extensive, unstable slope would continue to erode over
time and provide a public safety hazard.

Construction, Operation, and Maintenance Costs
No construction or maintenance costs would be incurred, aside from costs associated
with future stream restoration work that are anticipated to increase over time.

Reliability
The no-action alternative is not reliable in protecting water quality or preventing further
degradation of Blue Earth River, the west slope and downstream waters.

3       Preferred alternative project design
3.1      Preferred Alternative (Alternative 2)
The preferred alternative will restore segments of eroding stream banks within an
approximately 2,310-foot reach of Blue Earth River with access to a privately owned central
parcel available for project development (Attachment 2). The engineer’s opinion of
construction cost for this alternative is $25 million. Long-term maintenance costs are
generally low, as riprap is durable and resistant to erosive forces once installed. In-channel
maintenance is also anticipated to be minimal, as the intention of the project is to allow
the river to re-establish a new equilibrium through natural processes.

Channel and side slope restoration would occur after the removal of Rapidan Dam and will
be informed by two-dimensional hydraulic modeling and comparison of current
topography with pre-dam topography. Channel restoration would consist of grading the in-
 place materials and establishing stable channel side slopes. Slope and bank restoration
techniques include benching, channel bank cutting, and placing ﬁll material to create a
stable slope extending from the channel toe to the top of the existing scarp. The material
would be placed in compacted lifts. Filter aggregate and appropriately sized rip rap may be
used to stabilize select areas of the channel based on its hydraulic properties. Prior to the
west bank restoration, the river would be temporarily diverted to its main channel to isolate
the construction area. Restoration would likely occur on the east bank prior to the
diversion

Tree removal is necessary for grading portions of the west and east banks. Vegetation
utilizing native seed mixtures will be established after construction.

Unanticipated adverse impacts will be minimized by conducting in-water work outside of
DNR in-water work exclusion dates, March 15 through April 15. Equipment will be free of
aquatic plants/water/non-native animals/prohibited invasive species prior to placement in
any waters.

Surface water impacts will be minimized through implementation of the following
temporary best management practices:

   •   Rock construction entrances, silt fence, and other erosion protection features,
       would be implemented to minimize construction impacts.
   •   In-water work will occur during low to normal ﬂow conditions.
   •   Existing vegetation within the temporary workspace will be retained as practicable.
   •   Prior to ground disturbance, temporary sediment control measures (silt fence,
       sediment control log, rock construction entrance) will be installed and maintained
       as needed to prevent sediment transport off-site. If off-site sedimentation is
       observed work will be stopped and malfunctioning sediment control devices will be
       repaired, or alternative measures implemented. Accumulated sediment will be
       removed from behind sediment control logs and silt fence whenever accumulation
       reaches 1/3 of BMP height.
   •   Flow may be temporarily restricted to either side of the channel to facilitate
       construction and minimize construction impacts. Prior to the west bank restoration,
       water control measures would be adjusted to divert water toward the main channel
       of the river to facilitate construction.
   •   Coffer dams will be utilized to isolate the dam during removal.
   •   Dewatering and diversion will be utilized when and where practical. When any in-
       stream work is anticipated, one or more ﬂoating silt curtains or other BMPs will be
       placed to isolate the work area prior to the start of construction.
   •   The drawings identify locations where equipment access within and across the Blue
       Earth River channel is required to complete dam removal work
     •    Construction will be phased to minimize exposed soil. Exposed soil and temporary
         work areas will be stabilized with seed and erosion control blankets as soon as
         practicable.

4       Water quality parameters of concern
The proposed project is expected to restore the Blue Earth River to a more natural condition
by improving streambank stability and enhancing aquatic and riparian habitat. Because
some work will occur within the river channel, temporary increases in total suspended
solids and turbidity may occur during construction. Erosion and sediment control
measures will be implemented during construction to minimize sedimentation impacts.
The project is not expected to exacerbate existing watershed impairments. While short-
term construction-related impacts may occur, the project is designed to provide long-term
water quality beneﬁts by stabilizing the west and east banks, reducing erosion, and
decreasing sediment inputs to the Blue Earth River.

9      Indirect impacts
Indirect impacts from the project may include temporary impacts to aquatic life, wildlife
habitat, and hydrology. These impacts will be minimized by 1) using appropriate BMPs to
prevent erosion and control sediment during construction, 2) reseeding areas after
construction with native vegetation, 3) conducting in-water work outside of DNR in-water
work exclusion dates, March 15 through April 15.

It is not expected that the proposed project will negatively affect the water quality following
construction; rather, the proposed project will reduce erosion on the west and east banks
of the river. The project will use BMPs and work in water will follow DNR guidelines and best
management practices. Fill impacts have been minimized where practicable.

10     Loading and degradation to surface waters
There are no net increases in long-term loading or other degradations expected upon
completion of the project.

11     Comparison of existing and expected economic conditions and social
       services
11.1     Economic Gains or Losses Attributable to the Proposed Activity
Under existing conditions, ongoing streambank erosion due to the damaged Rapidan Dam
along Blue Earth River contributes to elevated total suspended solids and turbidity, which
degrades water quality and increases long-term management and maintenance costs for
downstream water resources.

The proposed project represents an upfront capital investment but is expected to generate
long-term economic beneﬁts by reducing future costs associated with sediment removal,
infrastructure protection, emergency stabilization, and downstream water quality
impairments. Rapidan Dam, a hydroelectric facility, has not generated electricity since
2019 and electricity demand has been met by other means; therefore, no impacts to
electrical service would occur nor are electrical rates anticipated to be affected by the
project. No long-term economic losses are anticipated as a result of the project. The
project is also expected to protect adjacent public and private property by stabilizing the
west and east banks, thereby preserving property values and reducing the potential need
for future repairs or emergency interventions.

11.2     Contribution to Social Services
The project area includes publicly accessible land within Rapidan Dam Park and
surrounding neighborhoods. By improving stream stability, water quality, and aquatic and
riparian habitats, the project supports recreational, aesthetic, and educational uses of the
river corridor. Improved environmental conditions enhance the value of parkland and

natural spaces.

11.3   Prevention or Remediation of Environmental or Public Health Threats
The proposed activity is designed to remediate existing environmental degradation caused
by ongoing west bank erosion and sediment transport. By reducing sediment and
associated nutrient loading, the project addresses stressors that impair aquatic life and
downstream waterbodies. Leaving the steep eroded bank on the west side of the river
channel would create a long-term public hazard. Restoring this area reduces the public
hazard and improves the environmental conditions.
11.4   Climate Change Considerations
The project design incorporates climate resilience by stabilizing streambanks and channel
features to better withstand higher peak ﬂows and increased precipitation intensity
associated with climate change. Native riparian vegetation establishment will improve
inﬁltration, provide shading to reduce thermal stress on aquatic systems, and enhance
long-term system adaptability. These measures are expected to reduce vulnerability to
future hydrologic extremes.

11.5   Trade-Offs Between Environmental Media
Short-term, localized increases in turbidity and total suspended solids may occur during
construction; however, these temporary impacts will be minimized through
implementation of best management practices and in-water work restrictions. These short-
term impacts are outweighed by long-term improvements to surface water quality, aquatic
habitat, aquatic life mobility, and sediment load reductions. No signiﬁcant, adverse, long-
term impacts to other environmental media (air, soil, or groundwater) are anticipated.

11.6   Value of the Water Resources
Blue Earth River is a major tributary to the Minnesota River. Its connected waterbodies
provide important ecological, recreational, and aesthetic value within the watershed.
Improving water quality and habitat conditions supports designated uses, protects
downstream lakes and wetlands, and contributes to overall watershed health. The
proposed project enhances these values by restoring natural processes and long-term
reducing pollutant loading.

11.7   Other Relevant Environmental, Social, and Economic Impacts
The preferred alternative is expected to result in net positive environmental and social
outcomes by improving aquatic and riparian habitat, supporting biodiversity, and
enhancing long-term sustainability of the river system. Temporary construction-related
impacts will be minimized through phased construction, erosion control measures, and
 restoration of disturbed areas. Overall, the proposed activity provides long-term
environmental, social, and economic beneﬁts compared to existing conditions.

Repairing or rehabilitating the dam to its original condition would require signiﬁcant public
investment with limited beneﬁt, particularly given the outdated purpose and lack of
modern utility for the structure. Conversely, removal would eliminate ongoing maintenance
and liability costs while supporting natural resource recovery.

Federal

                                                                                   1 Introduction
On behalf of Blue Earth County, Barr Engineering Co. (Barr) conducted a wetland and watercourse
delineation and an offsite hydrology review for the Rapidan Dam Removal Project (study area) in Blue
Earth County, Minnesota (Township 107 North, Range 27 West, Sections 5, 6, 7, and 8). The field effort
was conducted on June 30 - July 3, 2025.

A larger area that extends outside of the current study area was delineated during the July field effort.
The study area was revised to encompass a smaller footprint after field data were collected. Data
gathered outside of the study area can be provided upon request.

The goal of this project is to remove the failed Rapidan Dam in a way that minimizes impacts the Blue
Earth River and adjacent lands, reestablish the river channel in the vicinity of the dam, restore the west
embankment by reclaiming the lost property or designing other stable-slope solutions, and restore the
east embankment that will become exposed as part of the dam removal.

This wetland delineation report and offsite hydrology review has been prepared in accordance with the
U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) 1987 Wetland Delineation Manual (USACE 1987), the Regional
Supplement to the Corps of Engineers Wetland Delineation Manual: Midwest Region (USACE, 2010), the
Corps of Engineers and Board of Water and Soil Resources (BWSR) Guidance for Offsite
Hydrology/Wetland Determinations (USACE & BWSR, 2016), and the requirements of the Minnesota
Wetland Conservation Act (WCA) of 1991.

This report includes general environmental information (Section 2), offsite hydrology review (Section 3),
wetland delineation and classification methods (Section 4), descriptions of the delineated wetland areas
(Section 5), and a discussion of regulations and the administering authorities (Section 6). Tables 1-4
include mapped soil and aquatic resources, precipitation data, and a wetland summary. Figures 1-5
include Project Location, Topography, Mapped Aquatic Resources, Mapped Soil, and Wetland
Delineation Results. Figures 1B-5J include aerial imagery for each year identified. Appendix A includes

                                                                2 Environmental Setting

    2.1 Site Description
The study area includes approximately 38.7 acres along an approximately 3,149 foot reach of the Blue
Earth River. The Blue Earth River originally flowed under a bridge on County State Aid Highway (CSAH) 9
within the study area before the dam failed. After the failure, the bridge was removed due to structural
concerns. The study area is located on both public and private land and is mostly wooded with an area of
agricultural fields on the western side of the study area. The most significant land use has been the
Rapidan Dam structure, and stabilization of the riverbanks near the bridge area.

     2.2 Geology, Landform, and Topography
According to the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources (MnDNR) Ecological Classification System,
the study area is located in the North Central Glaciated Plains (251B) ecological section within the
Minnesota River Prairie (251Ba) ecological subsection. This subsection is characterized by thick deposits
of glacial till overlying bedrock primarily composed of clay, sandstone, and shale. Ground elevations in
the study area range from 944 to 814 feet above mean sea level (amsl). The lowest elevation is
associated with the channel of the Blue Earth River.

    2.3 Mapped Water Resources
The study area is located within the Minnesota River basin (major surface watershed #30), within the
Wetland Bank Service Area 9. The Blue Earth River flows north through the study area, where it
eventually outlets into the Minnesota River.

The National Wetlands Inventory (NWI) was developed by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) in
the late 1970s and updated by the MnDNR in 2013. The NWI identifies 16.3 acres of wetlands within the
study area (Figure 3). The NWI wetland community types include shallow marsh and non-vegetated
aquatic communities.

The MnDNR Public Water Inventory (PWI) identifies one public water course
(Blue Earth River, M - 055 - 076) and one public water basin (Rapidan Lake, 07008700) in the study area.

    2.4 Mapped Soil Resources
Soil data for the study area were obtained from the NRCS Web Soil Survey (2026). Web Soil Survey
identifies 7 mapped soils within the study area (Figure 4). Table 1 lists each soil series, hydric rating, total
area, and percent abundance. Approximately 10.6 percent of the area is mapped with soils classified as
hydric or predominantly hydric, while 58.9 percent of the soils are classified as non-hydric or
predominantly non-hydric and 30.5 percent is mapped as water.

Hydric soils are defined by the National Technical Committee for Hydric Soils (NTCHS) as soils that
formed under conditions of saturation, flooding, or ponding long enough during the growing season to
develop anaerobic conditions in the upper part (NRCS 1994). Under natural conditions, these soils are
either saturated or inundated long enough during the growing season to support the growth and
reproduction of hydrophytic vegetation. Soils are classified as hydric using the following rating:

    •   All Hydric (100%)
    •   Predominantly hydric (67%-99%)
    •   Partially hydric (>33%-<67%)
    •   Predominantly non-hydric (>0%-<34%)
    •   Non-hydric (0%)

    •    Not Cropped (NC)
    •    Standing Water (SW)
    •    Wetland Signature (WS)
    •    Normal Vegetative Cover (NV)
    •    No Soil Wetness (NSS)

Wetland status is determined by considering the percentage of wetland signature occurrences, as well as

                                                    4 Wetland Delineation Methods
4.1.1 Field Wetland Delineation
Wetlands within the study area were delineated and classified during the site visit on July 1-3, 2025.
Wetland determination data forms were completed for each field-delineated wetland (Appendix A).

Delineated wetlands were classified using the Eggers and Reed (2015) wetland plant community types,
the USFWS Circular 39 Classification System (Shaw and Fredine 1956), the Cowardin classification
system (Cowardin et al. 1979, and the Hydrogeomorphic (HGM) classification system (BWSR 2022).

Hydrologic conditions, vegetation, and soils were generally evaluated at each wetland and this
information was recorded in ArcGIS Field Maps and in the wetland determination data forms. Each
wetland data form represents a sampling point within a wetland; the wetland ID is identified on each data
form. All wetland sampled points in Appendix A end with a “W”, while all upland sample points end with a
“U”.

The wetland boundaries were mapped in the field using ESRI’s Field Maps app, paired with an external
Leica Geosystems FLX100 submeter GNSS receiver. The data was exported for use in ESRI’s ArcGIS
Pro Software.

When conducting the field delineation, sample sites were established in both wetland and upland areas
and observations were recorded electronically with BioApp software. BioApp is an application designed to
aid wetland delineators in collecting, analyzing, and organizing field data (BioApp Incorporated 2025).
Information including NRCS soil data, NWI data, wetland indicator status, and vegetation calculations
area automatically generated once the data is entered into the application. Additionally, the application
provides suggested hydric soil and hydrology indicators which are reviewed for applicability. The auto-
populated, suggested, and manually entered data within the application is then exported to a wetland
determination data form for the project. Once the data is exported from BioApp, the wetland determination
data forms were reviewed to check the accuracy of the information presented within the form.

Soil borings were collected at sample points in and around wetlands, to a depth of at least 20 inches
below the ground surface or until auger refusal by coarse fragments. Soil samples from each boring were
examined for the presence of hydric soil indicators using the NRCS hydric soil indicators (NRCS 2025;
Version 9.2). Soil colors (e.g., 7.6YR 4/2, etc.) were determined using a Munsell soil color chart and noted
on the wetland determination data forms.

Plant species at each sample site were identified and percent areal cover was estimated for each
species. Dominant species were determined using the 50/20 rule, and the corresponding wetland
indicator status of each plant species was recorded using the current National Wetland Plant List
(USACE 2022). Overall vegetation for each wetland community is described in Section 5.2.

 4.1.2 Field Watercourse Delineation
Drainages within the study area may be considered non-wetland Waters of the U.S. (WOTUS), as they
may not exhibit all parameters required for wetlands (i.e. predominance of hydrophytes, hydric soils, and
jurisdictional hydrology). Barr used the National Ordinary High Water Mark Field Delineation Manual for
Rivers and Streams, Final Version (USACE 2025) to delineated watercourse boundaries in the field by
documenting their Ordinary High-Water Mark (OHWMs), as determined according to the USACE
Regulatory Guidance Letter No. 05-05 (USACE 2005). USACE regulations set forth at 33 CFR 328.3(e)
defines the OHWM for purposes of the Clean Water Act lateral jurisdiction is the line on the shore
established by the fluctuations of water and indicated by physical characteristics including:

    •   Natural line impressed on the bank
    •   Shelving
    •   Changes in the character of soil
    •   Destruction of terrestrial vegetation
    •   Presence of litter and debris
    •   Wracking
    •   Vegetation matted down, bent, or absent
    •   Sediment sorting
    •   Leaf litter disturbed or washed away
    •   Scour
    •   Deposition
    •   Multiple observed flow events
    •   Bed and banks
    •   Water staining
    •   Change in plant community

5.2.1 Wetland C
This wetland is classified as a PUBG; shallow, open water community (Type 5). Based on review of aerial

location was inaccessible during the sight visit due to steep and unstable slopes; therefore, sample points
and datasheets were not collected for Wetland C.

Vegetation observed from the overlook area on the east side of the wetland indicates that this area is

 5.2.2 Wetland D
This wetland is classified as a fresh (wet) meadow community (Type 2). This fresh (wet) meadow
community is split between two different hydrogeomorphic (HGM) and Cowardin classifications. The
portion of the wetland that directly abuts the Blue Earth River has a riverine HGM and a PEM1B Cowardin
classification. This portion of the wetland is dominated by dock-leaf smartweed (Persicaria lapathifolia)
and barnyard grass (Echinochloa crus-galli) with sapling silver maple (Acer saccharinum) and witchgrass
(Panicum capillare) also present. The other portion of this fresh wet meadow community is associated
with a seep on a hillside and has a slope HGM classification and a PEM1D Cowardin classification. This
portion of the wetland is dominated by reed canary grass (Phalaris arundinacea) and dock-leaf
smartweed with orange jewelweed (Impatiens capensis), Allegheny monkey flower (Mimulus ringens),
and eastern cottonwood (Populus deltoides) saplings also present. Vegetation in this portion of the
wetland is disturbed due to the recent removal of construction mats in the temporary access road that
runs through part of this wetland.

Soil in the riverine HGM portion of this fresh (wet) meadow community at sample point RD10W consists
of 26 inches of 2.5Y 2.5/1 and 10YR 3/4 saturated silt loam with 2 percent 10YR 4/6 redoximorphic
concentrations. This soil profile meets the hydric soil indicator redox dark surface (F6). Primary hydrology
indicators include saturation and algal mat or crust. Secondary hydrology indicators include surface soil
cracks and FAC-neutral test.

Soil in the slope HGM portion of this fresh (wet) meadow community at sample point RD4W consists of 14
inches of 2.5Y 3/1 saturated mucky mineral soil with 5 percent 10YR 4/6 redoximorphic concentrations.
This soil profile meets the loamy mucky mineral (F1) hydric soil indicator. Primary hydrology indicators
include surface water of 3 inches, high water table, and saturation. Secondary hydrology indicators
include surface soil cracks and FAC-neutral test. Soil and hydrology in this portion of the wetland are
disturbed due to the recent removal of construction mats.

The wetland boundary in the field is defined by a change in topography from the riverbank and seepage
hillslope going into the summit at the top of the hillslope. The wetland boundary is further refined by a
change in vegetation from a community dominated by dock-leaf smartweed into an open area lacking
hydrology indicators and being dominated by reed canary grass and American burnweed (Erechtites
hieraciifolius) with stinging nettle (Urtica dioica) also present.

5.2.3 Wetland G
This wetland is primarily classified as a PEM1B, fresh (wet) meadow (Type 2) and abuts the bank of the
Blue Earth River with a riverine HGM classification. Part of this wetland extends upslope into a seepage
hillside and is associated with a groundwater fed seepage channel that flows into the river. A small
portion (approximately 0.04-acres) of this wetland is classified as a PEM1C, shallow marsh (Type 3). This
shallow marsh is a seepage pool that is higher in elevation than the edge of the riverbank. Dominant
vegetation in this wetland includes dock-leaf smartweed, curly dock (Rumex crispus) and reed canary
grass.

Soil in Wetland G at sample point RD9W consists of 36 inches of 2.5Y 2.5/1 moist silt loam with 5 percent
2.5Y 4/4 and 5 percent 2.5Y 4/3 redoximorphic concentrations. This soil profile meets the redox dark
surface (F6) hydric soil indicator. Secondary hydrology indicators include surface soil cracks and FAC-
neutral test. Other areas within the wetland have 1”-2” of surface groundwater flow from seepages. The
shallow marsh portion of this wetland has surface water 2 feet in depth and aquatic fauna.

                                                                   6 Regulatory Overview
The USACE regulates the dredge or placement of fill materials into wetlands that are adjacent to or are
hydrologically connected to interstate or navigable waters under the authority of Section 404 of the Clean
Water Act. If the USACE has jurisdiction over any portion of a project they may also review impacts to
wetland under the authority of the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA).

Filling, excavating, and draining wetlands are also regulated by the Wetland Conservation Act (WCA).
WCA is administered by the Local Government Unit (LGU), which is Blue Earth County. The Blue Earth
SWCD, MnDNR, and the USACE should be contacted before altering any aquatic resources. Delineated
wetland boundaries may be reviewed, if needed by the USACE and a WCA Technical Evaluation Panel
(TEP) consisting of representatives from the Minnesota Board of Water and Soil Resources (BWSR),
MnDNR, and Blue Earth County.
